title: The Second Vision Begins
sum: Chapters 37–71 open with a new title: "the second vision... the vision of wisdom." Enoch, traced back through Genesis 5 to Adam, says he received wisdom no one before him had been given, and a share in eternal life. He has three "parables" to tell the people of the earth: of those long ago and of those still to come.
This short preface introduces the most debated book inside 1 Enoch. It is the part with the Son of Man, the Chosen One and the Lord of Spirits, and the only part not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
readings: Read as prophecy
Ethiopian Orthodox readers take the preface at its word: Enoch, before the Flood, is given visions of the coming judge and the end of the world, meant for every generation, ours included.
Read as a Jewish book of its time

Most scholars read it as the work of a Jewish writer around the time of Jesus, who spoke in Enoch's name to give his visions the weight of the earliest prophet, as Daniel's visions were set in the Babylonian court.

views.E: Enoch is a true prophet, "the seventh from Adam" (Jude 14), and these parables are part of the Ge'ez Old Testament. The church reads the Son of Man and the Chosen One as Christ, whom Enoch foresaw.
views.H: The Book of Parables (Similitudes) is a separate work, added after the Book of the Watchers. It is missing from the Qumran fragments and has no surviving Greek. Most date it from the late first century BC to before AD 70; a few later.
views.N: Students of the New Testament read 37–71 for the Son of Man, the judge on "the throne of his glory" (Matthew 19:28; 25:31), the Messiah and the Chosen One, all in one Jewish text.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism did not keep the Parables; Jews know them today only through the Ethiopian church and modern scholarship. The hope for a heavenly judge and the exalted Enoch reappears in later mystical writing such as 3 Enoch.
views.W: Most churches read 37–71 as a Jewish witness to the hopes of Jesus' time: helpful for understanding the Gospels' language, but not Scripture, and to be tested by the Bible.

echoes: Genesis 5:3–24; Jude 14; Hebrews 11:5; Numbers 23:7; Daniel 7:9–14

settings.what: The title and preface of the Book of Parables
settings.to: "the people who live on the earth": those of old and those who come later
settings.when: before the three parables are told
settings.why: to present what follows as revealed wisdom, older than the Flood, and to warn every generation of the coming judgment
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.
views: Late first century BC to before AD 70, a Jewish work (the Enoch Seminar, Camaldoli 2005; Boccaccini, ed., 2007; Nickelsburg and VanderKam).
Still Jewish, but written toward the end of the first century AD (Knibb 1979); Mearns (1979) also argued for a first-century AD date.
A Jewish work of about AD 115–117, reading 56:5–7 against Trajan's Parthian war (Hindley 1968).
Written by a Christian about AD 270, which would explain its absence from Qumran (Milik 1976).
The words of Enoch himself, before the Flood.

title: Where Will the Sinners Live?
sum: The first parable opens with a question. When the community of the righteous appears, when the Righteous One appears, and when light shines on the chosen, where will the sinners go? Where will those who denied the Lord of Spirits rest? "It would have been better for them never to have been born."
The parable names its enemy at once: the kings, the powerful and "those who hold the land." They will not even be able to look at the faces of the holy ones, and no one will plead for them.

views.E: The Righteous One is Christ, who appears to judge; the chapter is a call to repent while there is time.
views.H: The chapter shows the social world of the writers: a small community oppressed by rulers and landowners, waiting for a reversal. "Those who hold the land" may point to the great estates of Herodian Judea.
views.N: The phrase "better never born" is used by Jesus of Judas (Matthew 26:24). The hope of the meek inheriting the land (Matthew 5:5) has the same shape.
views.W: A strong word of comfort to the oppressed and warning to the powerful, which the Bible shares (Luke 1:51–53; James 5:1–6); its date and setting are uncertain.

echoes: Psalm 1:4–6; Psalm 37:9–11; Matthew 26:24; Matthew 5:5; Luke 1:51–53; James 5:1–6

settings.what: The first parable
settings.to: the people of the earth (37:5); inside the parable, the righteous and the sinners are spoken of, not to
settings.when: the first of three parables
settings.why: to assure the righteous that their hidden faithfulness will be revealed, and to warn the powerful that their power will end
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Homes of the Righteous
sum: Enoch is snatched up by a cloud and a whirlwind to the far end of the heavens. There he sees the homes of the righteous dead, living with the angels and praying for people on earth. Under the wings of the Lord of Spirits they shine like fire.

Enoch longs to live there, and learns that his place has been waiting all along. He hears the angels who never sleep singing "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Spirits," until his face is changed and he can no longer look.

views.E: The vision shows the saints in God's presence praying for the world, which the Ethiopian church confesses; the song is the Sanctus sung in its liturgy.
views.H: Verse 1–2 seem to belong to the Watchers story and are out of place; the vision of the righteous dead with the angels is a Jewish picture of the afterlife before the resurrection.
views.N: Close parallels: the souls of the righteous in God's presence (Hebrews 12:22–24), the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8), and the Sanctus of Revelation 4:8.
views.J: The angels' song is the Kedushah of the synagogue prayers, here with "the Lord of Spirits" in place of "the LORD of Armies."
views.W: A beautiful picture of the life to come; churches differ on whether the departed pray for the living (see the card below).

echoes: 2 Kings 2:11; Isaiah 6:1–3; Psalm 91:4; Revelation 4:8; Revelation 5:8; Hebrews 12:22–24; Luke 9:29

settings.what: Enoch's vision of the homes of the righteous
settings.to: the readers of the parable; inside it, Enoch praises God (39:10, 12–13)
settings.when: after a whirlwind carries him to the end of the heavens
settings.why: to show that the righteous dead are safe with God and to model praise
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

traditions.q: Do the saints in heaven pray for people on earth, and may we ask them to?
views: Yes. The saints in heaven intercede for the church, and the faithful may ask for their prayers (Catechism 956, 2683).
Yes. The departed saints are alive in Christ and pray for the world; the faithful ask their intercession in the liturgy.
Yes. The saints and angels intercede, and passages like 1 Enoch 39:5 are read as part of Scripture's witness to it.
The saints in heaven pray for the church in general, but Scripture gives no command or promise for calling on them (Apology of the Augsburg Confession, article 21).
Christ is the only mediator; Scripture does not teach that the departed hear our prayers, and we pray to God alone (Westminster Confession 21.2).
Prayer is to God through Christ alone; asking the departed to pray is not taught in Scripture.

title: Four Faces Around the Throne
sum: After countless thousands of angels, Enoch sees four "faces" on the four sides of the Lord of Spirits. Each has a voice and a job. One blesses God; one blesses the Chosen One and the chosen; one prays for the people of the earth; and one drives away "the satans" who come to accuse them.
The angel of peace who guides Enoch gives their names: Michael, merciful and slow to anger; Raphael, over disease and wounds; Gabriel, over every power; and Phanuel, over repentance and hope.

views.E: The Ethiopian church honors these archangels, Phanuel among them, as the Bible's own witness to the angels around God's throne.
views.H: The list reflects Jewish angelology of the time: four angels of the presence, named, with offices. Phanuel replaces Uriel from 9:1 and 20:1–8.
views.N: Gabriel is "the one who stands before God" (Luke 1:19), and the accuser is thrown down in Revelation 12:10; both ideas appear here.
views.J: The four angels Michael, Gabriel, Uriel and Raphael surround God's throne in later Jewish prayers and midrash (Numbers Rabbah 2:10); Phanuel is replaced there by Uriel.
views.W: Most churches accept only the names Scripture gives, honoring Michael and Gabriel (and, for Catholics and Orthodox, Raphael).

echoes: Daniel 7:10; Isaiah 63:9; Luke 1:19; Tobit 12:15; Job 1:6–12; Zechariah 3:1–2; Revelation 12:10; 9:1

settings.what: The angel of peace explains the four faces
settings.by: the angel of peace, Enoch's guide
settings.when: after Enoch asks who the four are
settings.why: to teach that God's throne is surrounded by protectors: blessing, intercession and defense against accusers
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: Secrets of the Sky
sum: Enoch sees how God's kingdom is divided and how people's deeds are weighed on scales. He sees sinners driven out from among the chosen. Then the tour turns to the sky: lightning and thunder, the winds and the clouds, locked storehouses of hail and mist, and the paths of the sun and moon, which keep their oath and never stray.
The order of the sky is a lesson. The same sun and moon bring light to the righteous and darkness to sinners, and God, who separated light from darkness, appoints one judge over all.

views.E: God's order in creation teaches his faithfulness; the appointed judge is Christ.
views.H: A short version of the cosmic tours of 17–36 and the Astronomical Book (72–82), set into the first parable to show that the same God who orders the sky will judge.
views.N: Creation's order as a witness to God (Romans 1:20) and the judge appointed by God (Acts 17:31).
views.W: The picture of God's storehouses is the Bible's own poetic language (Job 38:22), not a science lesson.

echoes: Job 38:22–38; Psalm 135:7; Jeremiah 31:35–36; Daniel 5:27; Genesis 1:4; Acts 17:31

title: Wisdom Finds No Home
sum: A short poem breaks into the first parable. Wisdom looked for a place to live among people and found none, so she went back to heaven and sat among the angels. Then Wrongdoing came out of her rooms, found people who were not even looking for her, and moved in, welcome as rain in the desert.
readings: Read as a lament
The poem explains why the world is as bad as it is: people turned Wisdom away and took Wrongdoing in.
Read with the Bible's Wisdom poems
It answers Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24, where Wisdom comes to live among people. Here she is refused, as John 1:11 says of the Word.

views.E: Christ is the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) whom the world did not receive.
views.H: An independent wisdom poem, perhaps older than the Parables, inserted here. It reverses Sirach 24, where Wisdom finds a home in Israel's Torah.
views.N: The closest New Testament parallel is the prologue of John (John 1:10–11) and Jesus' lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).
views.J: Jewish wisdom tradition, from Sirach and Baruch 3–4 on, identified Wisdom with the Torah given to Israel; this poem is much bleaker.
views.W: Read as a poem about human rejection of God's wisdom, it agrees with Scripture.

echoes: Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–36; Sirach 24:1–12; Baruch 3:9–4:4; John 1:10–11; Matthew 23:37; 1 Corinthians 1:24

settings.what: A poem about Wisdom and Wrongdoing
settings.when: inserted between the visions of the sky
settings.why: to explain why the righteous are few and the wicked many: people refused Wisdom
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: Stars That Stand for the Righteous
sum: Enoch sees more lightnings and the stars, which God calls each by name, weighs on a fair scale and keeps in faithful order. When he asks what they are, the angel says the Lord of Spirits has shown him a picture: the stars are the names of the righteous who live on the earth and believe in the name of the Lord of Spirits.

views.E: God knows each believer by name, as he knows the stars.
views.H: Astronomy turned into a parable: the stars' faithful courses mirror the faithfulness of the righteous, a theme of the Enochic books.
views.N: The righteous "shine out like lights in the world" (Philippians 2:15); names written in heaven (Luke 10:20).
views.W: The image matches Daniel 12:3 and Psalm 147:4.

echoes: Isaiah 40:26; Psalm 147:4; Daniel 12:3; Philippians 2:15; Luke 10:20

settings.what: The angel explains the stars
settings.by: the angel who goes with Enoch
settings.when: after Enoch asks, "What are these?"
settings.why: to tell the faithful that God knows them by name and keeps them as faithfully as he keeps the stars
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: Stars That Become Lightning
sum: One verse closes the first parable: some of the stars rise and become lightning, and cannot leave that new form. Scholars are not sure whether this is a piece of ancient weather science or a warning that, like stars that leave their course, some can fall and not return.

views.H: A fragment, perhaps displaced; the first parable seems to end here without a formal close.
views.N: Jesus saw Satan "fall like lightning out of heaven" (Luke 10:18), and Jude 13 calls false teachers "wandering stars."
views.W: Too short and unclear to build any teaching on.

title: The Chosen One on the Throne of Glory
sum: The second parable is about those who deny the Lord of Spirits. They will go neither up to heaven nor down to the earth. Then God himself speaks: "On that day my Chosen One will sit on the throne of glory" and sort out their deeds.
God promises to change heaven and earth, to settle his chosen ones on the renewed earth, and to wipe the sinners off its face. This is the first time the Chosen One is enthroned as judge.

views.E: The Chosen One on the throne of glory is Christ, the judge of the living and the dead; the renewed earth is the new creation of the age to come.
views.H: The chapter fuses Isaiah's chosen servant (Isaiah 42:1) with a royal judge and with the new heavens and earth of Isaiah 65–66.
views.N: Only Matthew in the New Testament uses "the throne of his glory" for the Son of Man (Matthew 19:28; 25:31); the Parables use it here and often.
views.W: A Jewish hope for God's chosen judge and a renewed creation, which Christians see fulfilled in Christ (Revelation 21:1–5).

echoes: Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22; Matthew 19:28; Matthew 25:31; Luke 9:35; Revelation 21:1–5

settings.what: The second parable
settings.to: the people of the earth; within it, God speaks in the first person (45:3–6)
settings.when: the second of the three parables
settings.why: to announce the judge, the Chosen One, and the end of those who deny God, so that the oppressed would hold on
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

settings.what: God's announcement of the Chosen One
settings.to: the hearers of the parable, about the sinners and the chosen
settings.when: the day of judgment
settings.why: to promise the chosen a place on a renewed earth and to warn the deniers
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Head of Days and the Son of Man
sum: Enoch sees "one who had a head of days," with hair white like wool, and beside him another, whose face looks human and is full of grace like an angel's. This is Daniel 7's Ancient of Days and "one like a son of man," seen again.

Enoch asks who the second is. The angel answers: "This is the Son of Man who has righteousness." He reveals hidden things, he is chosen by the Lord of Spirits, and he will drag kings off their thrones, because they trust in their wealth, worship idols, deny the Lord of Spirits and persecute his faithful.
readings: Read as Jewish interpretation of Daniel

If the Parables are pre-Christian, as most scholars think, the chapter is the earliest known reading of Daniel 7:13 that treats "one like a son of man" as a single heavenly judge, not as a symbol of the holy people (Daniel 7:18).
Read as Christian prophecy
Ethiopian Orthodox readers, and many Christians who know the passage, read it as Enoch's vision of Christ beside the Father: human in appearance, heavenly in nature, the coming judge.

views.E: Enoch sees the Father and the Son. The Son of Man is Christ, both God and man, who will judge the kings of the earth.
views.H: The Parables combine Daniel's son of man, Isaiah's servant and the Davidic king into one figure. Whether "Son of Man" is a title here, or a description ("that human-like one"), is debated.
views.N: Jesus calls himself "the Son of Man" and speaks of coming with the clouds (Mark 14:62). The Parables show that some Jews of his time already read Daniel 7:13 of a single heavenly judge.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition later read Daniel's figure as the Messiah (Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a: "with the clouds of heaven" if Israel is worthy), but did not keep the Parables.
views.W: Important background for Jesus' title; it is not Scripture, and the New Testament's teaching about the Son of Man rests on Daniel and on Jesus' own words.

echoes: Daniel 7:9–14; Daniel 7:18; Mark 14:62; Revelation 1:13–14; Luke 1:51–53; Isaiah 14:11

settings.what: The angel explains the Son of Man
settings.by: one of the angels who goes with Enoch
settings.when: after Enoch asks who the human-like figure is, where he comes from and why he goes with the Head of Days
settings.why: to identify the coming judge and his targets: kings who trust in wealth and idols and who persecute the faithful
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

deep.h: Who is the Son of Man of the Parables?
deep.b:
The figure has four names in the Parables: the Son of Man, the Chosen One, the Righteous One and the Anointed One (Messiah). He is pictured as heavenly: chosen and hidden before creation (48:3, 6), sitting on the throne of glory (62:5), judging angels and kings (55:4; 69:27). He is also human-looking (46:1), and in 71:14 an angel tells Enoch, "You are the Son of Man."

Scholars read the evidence in several ways. (1) A Jewish heavenly Messiah, before Jesus. Most specialists today, following the Enoch Seminar (Camaldoli, 2005; Boccaccini, ed., 2007), date the Parables to about 40 BC–AD 70 and read the Son of Man as a pre-Christian Jewish figure, which helps explain how Jesus' hearers could understand his use of the title (Nickelsburg and VanderKam; Collins). (2) Jewish, but later. Knibb (1979) placed the Parables at the end of the first century AD, and Mearns (1979) also argued for a first-century AD date; Hindley (1968) dated them to AD 115–117, reading 56:5–7 against Trajan's Parthian war. On these views the Parables are Jewish, but too late to be a source for the Gospels. (3) A Christian composition or Christian additions. Because the Parables are missing from Qumran, Milik (1976) argued they were a Christian work of about AD 270; some older scholars thought the Son of Man passages were added by Christians. Few hold this today. One main reason is that a Christian writer would hardly identify the Son of Man with Enoch (71:14); another is that the Parables have no clear Christian marker, such as the cross or the name of Jesus. (4) Independent use of Daniel. Some (Casey) argue that "son of man" was not a fixed title in Judaism, and that the Parables and the Gospels each drew on Daniel 7 in their own way.

The Ethiopian Orthodox reading takes the book as prophecy given to Enoch before the Flood. On that reading the Son of Man, the Chosen One and the Messiah are Christ, foreseen long before his coming, and the Gospels' use of the title confirms the prophecy.

traditions.q: Who is the Son of Man of Enoch's Parables, and does the passage carry authority for Christians?
views: 1 Enoch is part of the Old Testament. The Son of Man, the Chosen One and the Messiah of the Parables are Christ, foreseen by Enoch, and the passage carries the authority of Scripture.
1 Enoch is not in the canon (Council of Trent, 1546). Catholic scholars read the Parables as a Jewish witness to the hopes that Christ fulfilled; Jesus' title rests on Daniel 7 and the Gospels.

Outside the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, Orthodox churches do not read 1 Enoch in the liturgy or count it as Scripture, though church fathers knew its traditions. Christ is the Son of Man of Daniel and the Gospels.
Only the 66 books are Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.2–3). Enoch may be read as a human writing that helps explain the background of the Gospels, but it has no authority to teach.

Many evangelical scholars value the Parables as background for Jesus' title, while insisting that the New Testament's Son of Man is defined by Jesus himself, not by Enoch (Bock and Charlesworth, eds., 2013).

title: The Prayer of the Righteous Goes Up
sum: The blood of the righteous and their prayers rise from the earth to God. The angels join them with one voice: may the prayer not be wasted, may justice be done, may the righteous not wait forever.
Then the Head of Days takes his seat, the books of the living are opened, and the holy ones rejoice, because the number of the righteous is complete, their prayer is heard and their blood is avenged.

views.E: The martyrs' prayer and God's answer, as in Revelation 6; the church honors its martyrs as those whose blood God will avenge.
views.H: Probably written for a community that had seen its members killed; the scene adapts Daniel 7:9–10's court.
views.N: Very close to Revelation 6:9–11 (souls under the altar, the full number, "how long?") and Luke 18:7–8.
views.W: Shares the Bible's assurance that God hears the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 3:7; Psalm 9:12).

echoes: Genesis 4:10; Daniel 7:9–10; Revelation 6:9–11; Revelation 20:12; Luke 18:7–8; 4 Ezra 4:35–37

settings.what: The prayer of the righteous and the opening of the books
settings.to: the readers, about the righteous who have been killed
settings.when: "in those days," the time just before the judgment
settings.why: to assure a suffering community that the blood of their dead has been heard and will be avenged
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Name Named Before the Sun
sum: Beside a spring of righteousness and many springs of wisdom, the Son of Man is "named" before the Lord of Spirits. His name was named before the sun and the stars were made. He will be a staff for the righteous, the light of the nations, the hope of the brokenhearted, and all on earth will bow before him.

He was chosen and hidden in God's presence before the world was made, and revealed to the holy. The kings who hold the land will hang their heads and burn like straw, for they denied the Lord of Spirits "and his Anointed One": the first time the book calls him the Messiah.

views.E: The Son of Man who exists before creation is the eternal Son, revealed in the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4); the chapter is read as a prophecy of the incarnation.
views.H: The chapter blends Isaiah's servant ("light of the nations," "hidden"), Psalm 2's anointed king and Proverbs 8's pre-existent Wisdom. Scholars debate whether pre-existence is real or "in God's plan."
views.N: Pre-existence and revelation are New Testament themes (John 1:1–3; 17:5; 1 Peter 1:20; Colossians 1:26); the Parables show a Jewish setting where such language made sense.
views.J: The rabbis taught that the name of the Messiah was among the things created before the world (Talmud, Pesachim 54a), close to 48:3.
views.W: Most Christian readers see in the chapter a remarkable Jewish anticipation of Christ, while reading it as human testimony, not revelation.

echoes: Proverbs 8:22–31; Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 49:2; Isaiah 49:6; Psalm 2:2; John 1:1–3; John 17:5; 1 Peter 1:20; Luke 2:32; Philippians 2:9–11

settings.what: The naming of the Son of Man
settings.to: the readers, about the righteous and the kings
settings.when: "at that hour," in the vision of the throne
settings.why: to show that the coming judge is older than creation, chosen by God, and the hope of the oppressed
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Spirit of Wisdom in the Chosen One
sum: Wisdom is poured out like water. The Chosen One stands in the presence of the Lord of Spirits, mighty in the secrets of righteousness. In him lives the spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge and might, the spirit of Isaiah 11, and he will judge the hidden things so that no one can speak an empty word before him.

views.E: Christ, on whom the Spirit rests (Isaiah 11:2; Luke 4:18), is the judge of hidden things.
views.H: The Chosen One is the Davidic "shoot" of Isaiah 11, joined here to the heavenly judge.
views.N: Compare the Spirit resting on Jesus at his baptism (Mark 1:10) and Paul's "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24).
views.W: A Jewish messianic reading of Isaiah 11, which Christians share.

echoes: Isaiah 11:1–5; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3; Matthew 12:36

title: A Door Left Open
sum: In those days the holy and chosen will be changed and filled with light. On the day of distress the righteous will win, and God will let "the others" see it, so that they repent and give up the works of their hands. In Dillmann's text they will have no honor (the EOTC Bible says they will), but they will be saved through God's name, for his mercy is great.
But there is a limit. After the judgment those who did not repent will be destroyed, and the Lord of Spirits says, "From now on I will have no mercy on them."

views.E: God's mercy reaches even those who repent at the last; the church calls all to repentance before the day comes.
views.H: A rare passage in apocalyptic writing that imagines a third group between the righteous and the wicked, probably Gentiles who turn to God at the end.
views.N: Compare the nations streaming to God (Isaiah 2:2–4; Revelation 21:24–26), the laborers of the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:1–16), and Paul's hope for the Gentiles (Romans 11:25).
views.W: Agrees with Scripture that God desires repentance (2 Peter 3:9) and that a day comes when it is too late (Hebrews 9:27).

echoes: Isaiah 2:2–4; Matthew 20:1–16; Luke 23:42–43; 2 Peter 3:9; Hebrews 9:27; Revelation 21:24–26

settings.what: A promise of change, with mercy for those who repent
settings.to: the readers: the holy and chosen, and "the others" who see their victory
settings.when: the day of distress before the final judgment
settings.why: to hold open a door of repentance for outsiders, while warning that it will close
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Earth Gives Back Its Dead
sum: The earth, Sheol and the place of destruction will give back what they hold: the dead will rise. The Chosen One will choose the righteous from among them, sit on his throne and pour out the secrets of wisdom.
Creation joins the joy: mountains leap like rams, hills skip like lambs, the angels' faces shine, and the chosen walk on a renewed earth.

views.E: The resurrection of the dead, confessed in the Creed, is foretold here by Enoch.
views.H: One of the clearest statements of bodily resurrection in Jewish literature before the New Testament, building on Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2.
views.N: Revelation 20:13 and John 5:28–29 are very close; so is 4 Ezra 7:32 from about AD 100.
views.J: Resurrection became a central Jewish belief; the Mishnah says that whoever denies it has no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1).
views.W: Agrees with the Bible's teaching on the resurrection.

echoes: Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:13; John 5:28–29; Psalm 114:4–6; 4 Ezra 7:32

settings.what: The resurrection and the Chosen One's reign
settings.to: the readers, the righteous who fear death
settings.when: "in those days": the end
settings.why: to promise that death will not keep the righteous, and that they will live on a renewed earth
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Mountains of Metal
sum: Carried west by a whirlwind, Enoch sees six mountains: iron, copper, silver, gold, soft metal and lead. The angel explains that they serve the authority of the Anointed One, and that all of them will melt like wax before the Chosen One.
In those days no one will be saved by gold or silver, no iron will be made for war, and no one will want bronze, tin or lead. All these things will vanish when the Chosen One appears.

views.E: The kingdoms and wealth of the world give way to Christ's kingdom, as in Daniel 2.
views.H: The metals stand for wealth and weapons, the arts that Azazel taught (8:1). The vision is an answer to the powerful, whose power rests on metal.
views.N: Compare the stone cut without hands (Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45) and the fall of Babylon's wealth (Revelation 18:11–17).
views.W: Shares the prophets' teaching that wealth will not save on the day of the LORD (Zephaniah 1:18).

echoes: Daniel 2:31–45; Micah 1:4; Psalm 97:5; Zephaniah 1:18; Isaiah 2:4; Revelation 18:11–17

settings.what: The angel explains the mountains of metal
settings.when: after Enoch asks what he has seen in secret
settings.why: to show that the wealth and weapons of the powerful will be useless before the Anointed One
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Valley That Is Never Full
sum: Enoch sees a deep valley, open wide. The nations bring gifts to the Chosen One, yet the valley is never filled. The sinners who crushed others will be driven off the earth, and the angels of punishment are already preparing the tools of Satan for the kings.
After this the Righteous and Chosen One will make the house of his congregation appear, the mountains will be flattened, and the righteous will rest from the sinners.

views.E: The house of his congregation is the church, which Christ gathers; the valley is the place of judgment.
views.H: The valley draws on the cursed valley by Jerusalem (27:1–3), the Hinnom Valley that gave its name to Gehenna.
views.N: Gehenna in the Gospels (Mark 9:43–48) and the gifts of the nations (Matthew 2:11; Revelation 21:26).
views.W: Images of judgment and gathering that the Bible also uses.

echoes: Joel 3:2; Joel 3:12; Jeremiah 7:31–32; Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 40:4; Mark 9:43–48

settings.what: The angel explains the tools of punishment
settings.when: after Enoch asks for whom the tools are being prepared
settings.why: to assure the oppressed that the kings' punishment is already being prepared, and that their gathering will appear
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: Chains for Azazel's Armies
sum: In another valley burning with fire, the kings and the powerful are thrown in. The angels forge iron chains for the armies of Azazel, and on the great day Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and Phanuel will throw them into the furnace, because they served Satan and led the earth astray.

Then, suddenly, the scene becomes the Flood: the waters above the heavens and below the earth, male and female, rush together and destroy all who live on the dry land. Most scholars think 54:7–55:2 is a piece of a Noah book.

views.E: The fallen angels will be punished at the last judgment, as Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 also teach; the Flood is a pattern of that judgment.
views.H: Two sources meet: the Parables' judgment of the kings and angels, and a Noah tradition about the Flood (54:7–55:2).
views.N: Jude 6, 2 Peter 2:4–5 and 1 Peter 3:19–20 join the fallen angels and the Flood in the same way.
views.J: The male and female waters reappear in later rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah 13:13).
views.W: The judgment of fallen angels has New Testament support; the details of Azazel and the four archangels do not.

echoes: Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4–5; 1 Peter 3:19–20; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 1:6–7; Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10

settings.what: The angel explains the chains, then the Flood
settings.when: in the vision of the burning valley
settings.why: to show that the fallen angels and their human allies face the same judgment, and that the Flood was a first judgment and a promise
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

title: God's Oath After the Flood
sum: After the Flood the Head of Days changes his mind: he destroyed the dwellers of the earth for nothing. He swears by his great name never to do it again and puts a sign in the heavens, a pledge as long as heaven is above the earth.

But judgment is not cancelled, only reshaped. God will seize the guilty by the hand of angels, and the mighty kings will be forced to watch the Chosen One on God's throne judge Azazel and all his armies.

views.E: God's covenant with Noah and his final judgment through Christ.
views.H: A retelling of Genesis 8:21–9:17 that ends by pointing to the final judgment.
views.N: 2 Peter 3:5–7 sets the Flood beside the coming judgment by fire.
views.W: Matches the Noah covenant of Genesis 9; the claim that the Flood was "for nothing" goes beyond Genesis.

echoes: Genesis 6:6; Genesis 8:21–22; Genesis 9:12–17; Isaiah 54:9; 2 Peter 3:5–7; 1 Corinthians 6:3

settings.what: God's oath and warning to the kings
settings.by: the Head of Days (the Lord of Spirits)
settings.to: the people of the earth, and then the mighty kings (55:4)
settings.when: after the Flood, looking ahead to the last judgment
settings.why: to promise that the world will not be destroyed by water again, and to warn the kings that the Chosen One will judge them
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Parthians and the Medes
sum: Angels with nets and chains go to throw the fallen angels' beloved ones into the valley. Then angels stir up the kings of the east, the Parthians and the Medes. They come like lions and wolves and trample the land of the chosen.
But the city of the righteous stops their horses. The invaders turn on one another until the dead are past counting, and Sheol opens its mouth and swallows them in front of the chosen.

views.E: A prophecy of the attack of the nations on God's people at the end, like Gog and Magog.
views.H: The only clear historical name in the Parables. Many date the book after the Parthian invasion of 40 BC; the passage reworks Ezekiel 38–39.
views.N: Revelation 9:14–16 and 16:12 have armies from the Euphrates; Revelation 20:8–9 the nations surrounding "the beloved city."
views.J: Later rabbinic sayings also linked Persian armies in the land with the coming of the Messiah (Lamentations Rabbah 1:41, on the Persian horses).
views.W: A vision in the style of Ezekiel 38–39; its historical reference helps date the book.

echoes: Ezekiel 38:1–23; Ezekiel 39:1–6; Zechariah 14:2–3; Revelation 9:14–16; Revelation 16:12; Revelation 20:8–9; Numbers 16:30–33

settings.what: The angel of peace on the angels of punishment and the invasion
settings.when: in the vision of the angels with nets
settings.why: to promise that the invasion from the east will fail before the city of the righteous
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.
views: Remembers the Parthian capture of Jerusalem in 40 BC and promises that a new attack will fail (Greenfield and Stone; Nickelsburg and VanderKam).
Reworks Ezekiel 38–39 and gives no firm date (Erho).

title: The Wagons From East and West
sum: The second parable ends with another army: wagons full of people, carried on the wind from the east and the west. Heaven notices the noise, the pillars of the earth shake, and the sound travels from one end of the world to the other in a single day.
These are probably the scattered people of Israel coming home. The parable closes with everyone bowing down to the Lord of Spirits.

views.E: The gathering of God's scattered people into his kingdom at the end.
views.H: The return of the Jews of the dispersion, a hope from Isaiah 49 and 60, placed right after the defeat of the invaders in chapter 56.
views.N: Compare the gathering of the chosen from the four winds (Mark 13:27) and many coming "from east and west" (Matthew 8:11).
views.W: Shares the prophets' hope that God will gather his people.

echoes: Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 49:22; Isaiah 60:4; Isaiah 66:20; Matthew 8:11; Mark 13:27

title: The Light of Eternal Life
sum: The third parable begins with a blessing: "Blessed are you, the righteous and the chosen, for your lot will be glorious." They will live in the light of the sun and in the light of eternal life, with days that never end.
Darkness is destroyed first, and light stands firm before the Lord of Spirits forever. The chapter is a short song before the third parable's visions of judgment.

views.E: The light of the kingdom, where Christ is the lamp (Revelation 21:23).
views.H: Light stands for salvation and life, as in Isaiah 60:19–20 and Daniel 12:3.
views.N: Before the New Testament, "eternal life" appears in Daniel 12:2, 2 Maccabees 7:9, Psalms of Solomon 3:12, the Community Rule from Qumran (1QS 4:7) and here; it becomes central in John's Gospel.
views.W: Agrees with the Bible's picture of eternal life in God's light.

echoes: Isaiah 60:19–20; Daniel 12:2–3; Matthew 5:3–12; John 8:12; Revelation 21:23; Revelation 22:5

settings.what: The third parable
settings.to: the people of the earth; within it, the righteous and the chosen are blessed (58:2)
settings.when: the last of the three parables
settings.why: to promise eternal light to the chosen and to show the final judgment of kings and angels by the Son of Man
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: Lightning for Blessing or for Curse
sum: Enoch sees the secrets of the lightning and the thunder. They are not blind forces: they flash and crash for blessing or for curse, as the Lord of Spirits commands.
Many scholars think this short chapter belongs with the astronomy of chapters 41–44 and the weather lore of chapter 60.

views.E: God rules nature and uses it for mercy and for judgment.
views.H: A piece of cosmic lore, perhaps moved here from another place in the Enoch tradition.
views.N: Compare the lightning and thunder from God's throne in Revelation 4:5.
views.W: Shares the Bible's belief that God rules the weather (Job 37:1–13).

echoes: Job 36:29–33; Job 37:1–13; Psalm 29:3–9; Psalm 135:7; Revelation 4:5

title: A Vision From Noah's Book
sum: Suddenly the date is "the five hundredth year... in the life of Enoch," though Noah was 500 years old in Genesis 5:32, and the speaker calls Enoch "my grandfather." This is a Noah fragment. Heaven shakes, the Head of Days sits on his throne, and the seer falls on his face until Michael's angel raises him up.

Michael warns that God's patience is coming to an end. Then the seer learns of two monsters: Leviathan, a female, in the sea, and Behemoth, a male, in a desert named Dendayn. An angel lists the spirits of the winds, thunder, hail, frost, snow, mist, dew and rain, each with its own storehouse and angel.
readings: Read as one book
Ethiopian readers take the chapter as part of Enoch's book, which Noah later received and in places added to (68:1).
Read as an inserted fragment

Most scholars think chapters 60 and 65–69:25 come from a lost "Book of Noah" and were placed into the Parables by an editor, which explains why "Enoch" in 60:1 and "my grandfather" in 60:8 do not fit together.

views.E: The Flood and the final judgment are both God's work; Leviathan and Behemoth are creatures God made and controls (Job 40–41).
views.H: A Noah fragment. Leviathan and Behemoth are old Canaanite chaos monsters tamed into creatures of the Creator, and the weather spirits reflect the angel lore of Jubilees 2:2.
views.N: Revelation's dragon and beasts from the sea and land (Revelation 13:1, 11) share the same roots.
views.J: In later Jewish tradition Leviathan and Behemoth become food for the righteous at the messianic banquet (4 Ezra 6:49–52; 2 Baruch 29:4; Talmud, Bava Batra 74b–75a).
views.W: The monsters and weather spirits go beyond the Bible's teaching, though the Bible also names Leviathan and Behemoth.

echoes: Genesis 5:32; Job 40:15–24; Job 41:1–34; Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; Job 38:22–30; 4 Ezra 6:49–52; 2 Baruch 29:4; Revelation 13:1; Revelation 13:11

settings.what: The Noah vision of the shaking heaven and the two monsters
settings.by: Noah (the speaker, who calls Enoch his grandfather), with Michael and another angel speaking to him
settings.when: "in the five hundredth year": in Noah's life, just before the Flood
settings.why: to show that the Flood and the last judgment come from a patient God whose mercy has a limit, and that the monsters and the weather are his to command
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.
views: An editor placed a piece of a Noah apocalypse here (Charles; Nickelsburg and VanderKam).
The Ethiopian reading: Noah received Enoch's book and added to it (68:1).

settings.what: Michael's warning
settings.when: after the seer collapses at the sight of the shaking heaven
settings.why: to explain that God's mercy and patience have lasted until now but that the day of judgment is prepared
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

settings.what: The angel who shows hidden things
settings.when: after the seer asks about the monsters
settings.why: to show that every part of nature has its appointed spirit and obeys God, and that the monsters wait for the day of judgment
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

title: The Chosen One Judges the Angels
sum: Angels are given long measuring cords and fly north. They will measure out the homes of the righteous and bring back even those lost in deserts, swallowed by fish or eaten by animals, so that no one is lost on the day of the Chosen One.

Then the Lord of Spirits seats the Chosen One on the throne of his glory, and he judges the works of the holy ones in heaven, weighing their deeds on scales. All the angels, cherubim, seraphim and ophanim, and the chosen in the garden of life, join in one great blessing.

views.E: Christ judges angels and men, and all creation praises the Holy Trinity; the church joins this heavenly praise in the liturgy.
views.H: The measuring cords combine the measuring of Jerusalem (Zechariah 2:1–5; Ezekiel 40) with the gathering of the dead for resurrection.
views.N: Paul says believers will judge angels (1 Corinthians 6:3); Revelation 11:1 and 21:15 use measuring rods; Revelation 20:13 has the sea give up its dead.
views.W: A vision of the judgment and the gathering of all the dead, close to Revelation.

echoes: Zechariah 2:1–5; Ezekiel 40:3; Revelation 11:1; Revelation 21:15; Revelation 20:13; 1 Corinthians 6:3; Isaiah 6:2; Ezekiel 1:15–21

settings.what: The angel explains the measuring cords
settings.by: the angel who goes with Enoch
settings.when: after Enoch asks why the angels took the cords
settings.why: to promise that no righteous person is lost, whatever happened to their body
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

settings.what: The song of all heaven
settings.by: all the angels and the chosen, with one voice
settings.when: after the Chosen One is enthroned
settings.why: to show all creation praising God because the judge has taken his seat
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Kings Before the Throne
sum: God commands the kings and the powerful to open their eyes and recognize the Chosen One. They see him sitting on the throne of his glory. Pain seizes them, like a woman in labor, when they see "that Son of a Woman" on the throne. They fall on their faces and beg for mercy, but the Lord of Spirits drives them out, and the angels of punishment take them.

The righteous are saved. They will live with that Son of Man, eat with him, lie down and get up with him forever, and put on the clothing of life. This chapter is the closest the Parables come to the Gospels' scene of the Son of Man judging the nations (Matthew 25:31–46).
readings: Read as Jewish background
The Son of Man on the throne of glory judging kings is a Jewish hope of the late Second Temple period. Jesus and the Gospel writers spoke into this world of ideas.
Read as fulfilled in Christ
Ethiopian Orthodox and many Christian readers see here the last judgment of Matthew 25, with the Son born of a woman (Galatians 4:4) on the throne.
Read as Christian influence
A few scholars think the parallels with Matthew are so close that the Parables may have been shaped by Christian ideas, or that both depend on one source.

views.E: The Son of a Woman is Christ, born of the Virgin Mary; the meal with him is the heavenly banquet that the Eucharist anticipates.
views.H: The scene reworks Isaiah 52–53, where kings shut their mouths at the exalted servant, and Daniel 7. Whether "Son of a Woman" is original or a slip for "son of a man" is debated (see the variant at 62:5).
views.N: Matthew alone has the Son of Man taking "his seat on the throne of his glory" (Matthew 19:28; 25:31). Some scholars think Matthew knew the Parables or the ideas behind them; others see only a shared reading of Daniel 7.
views.J: The eternal meal of the righteous is a Jewish image of the world to come (Isaiah 25:6); later rabbis said the world to come has no eating or drinking (Talmud, Berakhot 17a).
views.W: A striking parallel to Matthew 25; most churches read it as background that shows how Jesus' words would have been heard, not as Scripture.

echoes: Isaiah 13:8; Isaiah 52:13–15; Daniel 7:13–14; Matthew 19:28; Matthew 25:31–46; Matthew 26:64; Galatians 4:4; Revelation 6:15–17; Revelation 19:9; Isaiah 25:6

settings.what: God's summons to the kings
settings.to: the kings, the mighty, the high ones and those who hold the land
settings.when: the day of judgment
settings.why: to make the powerful face the judge they despised, and to assure the oppressed that they will be vindicated
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.
views: The kings and landowners are the Herods and the Roman-backed elite of Judea (Nickelsburg and VanderKam).
The kings are foreign rulers in general, as in Isaiah 52:15 (Charles).

deep.b:
The parallels between 1 Enoch 62 and Matthew do not settle when the Parables were written; that rests mainly on the historical hints (56:5–7; 67:8–13) and on their absence from Qumran. What the parallels bear on is the direction of borrowing, if there was any.

ParablesNew TestamentHow strong?
The Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory (62:5; 69:29)The Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory (Matthew 19:28; 25:31)Strong: the exact phrase, found nowhere else in the Gospels. Luke's version of 19:28 lacks it (Luke 22:30), so it looks like Matthew's own wording, and 25:31–46 is found only in Matthew.
All judgment is given to the Son of Man (69:27)The Father has given the Son authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man (John 5:22, 27)Strong in idea: judgment handed over to a figure called the Son of Man.
The kings and the mighty plead for mercy and are driven out (62:9–12)The nations gathered before him, some sent away (Matthew 25:32, 41, 46)Moderate: the same scene, but with different people judged.
Pain like a woman giving birth (62:4)The beginning of labor pains (Matthew 24:8)Weak: shared biblical imagery (Isaiah 13:8), not evidence of borrowing.
The righteous eat with him forever (62:14)Many will eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11)Weak: a common picture of the age to come (Isaiah 25:6).

Dating. Most scholars, with the Enoch Seminar, date the Parables between about 40 BC and AD 70. Knibb and Mearns placed them later in the first century AD, Hindley about AD 115–117, and Milik, as a Christian work, about AD 270. Dependence. These are separate questions. Some who date the Parables early think Matthew or his sources knew them, pointing to the phrase Matthew adds to his sources. Others who also date them early (Collins; Casey in his own way) see no direct borrowing, only a shared reading of Daniel 7. Those who date the Parables late, or think the Son of Man passages are Christian, can have the influence run from the Gospels to Enoch. The Ethiopian Orthodox reading: Enoch's prophecy came first, and the Gospels confirm what Enoch foresaw.

title: Too Late to Repent
sum: Handed over to the angels of punishment, the kings beg for a little rest so they can worship and confess. They praise "the Lord of kings" and admit that they trusted in the scepter of their kingdom. But they find no rest: light has passed away from them, and darkness is their home.
Their confession is true, but too late. They go down into Sheol, ashamed before that Son of Man, and God declares: this is the law for the mighty.

views.E: A warning to repent now, while there is time (2 Corinthians 6:2).
views.H: The kings' confession is a dramatic reversal: those who ruled must now say what the oppressed always believed. It echoes Wisdom of Solomon 5:3–13.
views.N: Compare the rich man in Hades (Luke 16:19–31) and the kings who hide from the Lamb (Revelation 6:15–17).
views.W: Agrees with the Bible that there is a time when it is too late (Hebrews 12:17), while most churches teach that God's mercy is open to all who repent in this life.

echoes: Wisdom of Solomon 5:3–13; Luke 16:19–31; Revelation 6:15–17; 2 Corinthians 6:2; Hebrews 12:17; Philippians 2:10–11

settings.what: The kings' confession
settings.to: the Lord of Spirits, and then themselves (63:10)
settings.when: after they are handed over to the angels of punishment
settings.why: to show the oppressed that the powerful will one day confess the truth they denied, though it will be too late
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: The Angels Who Taught What Was Hidden
sum: Enoch sees other forms hidden in the place of punishment. An angel tells him: these are the angels who came down from heaven and revealed hidden things to humans and led them into sin. The two verses recall the Watchers story (see 6:1–8:4).

views.E: The fallen angels who corrupted humanity will be judged.
views.H: A short link between the kings' judgment and the Noah material that follows, joining human and angelic sinners.
views.N: Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of the angels who left their place.
views.W: The fall of angels has New Testament support; the details come from the Watchers story.

echoes: Genesis 6:1–4; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4

title: Noah Cries Out to Enoch
sum: Noah sees the earth tilt and knows its destruction is near. He goes to the ends of the earth and cries three times to his grandfather Enoch. Enoch comes, and the earth trembles.

Enoch explains: the people have learned the angels' secrets, sorcery, spells and the casting of idols, and so the Flood will come. There is no way back for those who taught them. But Noah is pure and will be kept, and righteous offspring will come from him.

views.E: God saves the righteous from judgment, as he saved Noah and as he saves the church through Christ (1 Peter 3:20–21).
views.H: Another Noah fragment, close to the story of Noah's birth in 106–107 and to the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran.
views.N: Noah as a pattern of salvation in judgment (Matthew 24:37–39; Hebrews 11:7; 2 Peter 2:5).
views.W: Shares Genesis' picture of Noah as righteous (Genesis 6:9); the conversation with Enoch is outside the Bible.

echoes: Genesis 6:9; Genesis 6:11–13; Matthew 24:37–39; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20–21; 2 Peter 2:5

settings.what: The Noah fragments
settings.by: Noah (the speaker), reporting Enoch's words and visions
settings.when: just before the Flood
settings.why: to join the story of the Flood to the story of the last judgment, so that the Flood becomes a pattern for the end
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

settings.what: Enoch's answer to Noah
settings.to: Noah, his great-grandson (whom the text calls "my son")
settings.when: after Noah's three cries
settings.why: to explain why the Flood is coming and to promise that Noah and his offspring will be kept
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

title: The Angels Over the Waters
sum: Noah is shown the angels of punishment, ready to release the waters under the earth. But God orders them to hold back and keep watch, for now. Then Noah leaves Enoch's presence.

views.E: God holds back judgment until the right time, giving time for repentance.
views.H: A short scene that prepares for the Flood, with angels in charge of the waters as in chapter 60.
views.N: Compare the four angels holding back the winds (Revelation 7:1–3).
views.W: Shares the Bible's picture of God's patience before judgment (1 Peter 3:20).

echoes: Genesis 7:11; Revelation 7:1–3; 1 Peter 3:20

title: The Valley of Fire and the Healing Waters
sum: God speaks to Noah: his lot is without blame. The angels are building a wooden ark, and Noah's offspring will fill the earth. The angels who taught wrongdoing will be locked in a burning valley in the west, among mountains of metal.

From that valley flow hot waters mixed with fire and sulfur. They serve the kings and the powerful as baths for healing, yet they are a sign of the punishment waiting for them. One day the waters will change and burn forever. Michael adds that the judgment of the angels is a witness against the kings.

views.E: God's patience and judgment: the healing waters show mercy now, and their change shows the end.
views.H: The hot springs are probably real places: Callirrhoe near the Dead Sea, where Herod the Great went for treatment shortly before he died in 4 BC (Josephus, Jewish War 1.657). Many scholars use this to date the Parables.
views.N: The lake of fire for the devil and his angels (Revelation 20:10; Matthew 25:41).
views.W: A vivid local picture of judgment; the date clue is important for historians.

echoes: Genesis 6:14–16; Genesis 19:24; Matthew 25:41; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 20:10; Isaiah 66:24

settings.what: God's word to Noah
settings.when: before the Flood
settings.why: to assure Noah that he and his offspring will be saved and the earth filled again
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

settings.what: The burning valley and the waters
settings.when: before the Flood, looking ahead to the last judgment
settings.why: to show that the punishment of the angels is a warning to the kings, who use the waters for healing and still do not believe
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.
views: A pointed reference to Herod the Great's last treatment (Charles; Nickelsburg and VanderKam).
Hot springs and sulfur are a common picture of judgment, and the passage need not point to one king.

title: Michael and Raphael on the Judgment
sum: Enoch gives Noah the book of the parables. Then Michael speaks to Raphael: the judgment of the angels is so harsh that it makes him tremble. Who could bear it?
Yet Michael will not take their side before the Lord. They acted as if they were the Lord, and their judgment is theirs alone, forever.

views.E: Even the angels tremble at God's justice.
views.H: A rare glimpse of angels' feelings, perhaps meant to stress how serious the Watchers' sin was.
views.N: Compare "The demons believe it as well, and they shiver with fear" (James 2:19) and the angels who left their place (Jude 6).
views.W: An interesting picture of the angels; it goes beyond the Bible.

echoes: Jude 6; Jude 9; James 2:19; Daniel 10:13

settings.what: Michael to Raphael
settings.when: before the Lord of Spirits
settings.why: to show that the angels' sin was so grave that even Michael will not plead for them
settings.readers: Two layers. First, the readers of an older Noah tradition (a lost "Book of Noah"), probably Jewish and of unknown date, perhaps earlier than the Parables. Then the Parables' own readers, a Jewish group probably of the late first century BC or the first century AD, for whom an editor set the Flood beside the coming judgment of the kings.

title: The Names, the Oath and the Son of Man
sum: A list names the leaders of the fallen angels and what each taught: Yeqon led the angels astray, Asbeel gave them bad advice, Gadreel led Eve astray and taught weapons, Penemue taught writing with ink and papyrus, Kasdeya taught the blows of demons.

Then comes the hidden oath, through which heaven was hung, the earth founded and the sea given its limit, and by which the stars and the weather keep their courses. At the end, the angels rejoice because "the name of that Son of Man" has been revealed. He sits on the throne of his glory, all judgment is given to him, and evil passes away. This closes the third parable.

views.E: The Son of Man to whom all judgment is given is Christ (John 5:22, 27), revealed to the saints.
views.H: The list combines two lists of Watchers (compare 6:7). The oath is a hymn to the order of creation; 69:26–29 returns to the Parables' main theme.
views.N: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22; compare John 5:27).
views.J: The hidden name and oath that hold creation together resemble Jewish speculation about the divine name and creation (Sefer Yetzirah; Talmud, Sukkah 53b on the name that stopped the deep).
views.W: The ending is striking background for John 5; the names and the oath belong to Enoch's tradition alone.

echoes: Genesis 3:1–6; Job 38:8–11; Jeremiah 5:22; Psalm 104:5–9; Psalm 147:4; Daniel 7:14; John 5:22; John 5:27

settings.what: The hymn of the oath
settings.when: after the hidden name and oath are put in Michael's hand
settings.why: to show that the same power that keeps creation in order will also bring the judgment
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

settings.what: The revelation of the Son of Man's name
settings.when: at the close of the third parable
settings.why: to end all three parables with the judge on his throne and evil gone

title: Enoch Is Taken Up
sum: The book's first epilogue: while Enoch was still alive, his name was lifted up into the presence of that Son of Man and of the Lord of Spirits. He was taken on the chariots of the spirit and was no longer counted among humans.
He is set between the north and the west, where angels measure the place for the chosen, and he sees the first fathers and the righteous who have lived there from the beginning.

views.E: Enoch was taken to God without dying (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5), and will return as one of the two witnesses (Revelation 11:3).
views.H: The epilogue explains Genesis 5:24. Whether Enoch goes into the presence of the Son of Man, or becomes him (71:14), depends on a variant here (see the variant at 70:1).
views.N: Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was taken so that he did not see death.
views.J: Later Jewish mystical tradition made the taken-up Enoch into Metatron, the highest angel (3 Enoch 3–16).
views.W: Agrees with Genesis 5:24 and Hebrews 11:5 that Enoch was taken; the details are outside the Bible.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11; Hebrews 11:5; Revelation 11:3; 3 Enoch 3:1–2

settings.what: The epilogue: Enoch's ascent
settings.by: the narrator, then Enoch in the first person (70:3)
settings.when: after the three parables
settings.why: to explain how Enoch left the earth and what he saw, and to set up chapter 71
settings.readers: A Jewish group in the land of Israel, probably in the late first century BC or the first century AD (the date is debated), who called themselves "the righteous" and "the chosen" and felt crushed by kings, the powerful and the landowners.

title: "You Are the Son of Man"
sum: Enoch's spirit is carried up. He sees two rivers of fire, and Michael leads him to the secrets of heaven. In the heaven of heavens he sees a house of crystal with tongues of fire, guarded by those who never sleep, and the Head of Days comes out with Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and Phanuel. Enoch falls on his face and his spirit is changed.

Then an angel greets him: "You are the Son of Man who was born for righteousness." Those who walk in his path will live with him forever. This is the most surprising sentence in the Parables, and one of the most debated in all of 1 Enoch.
readings: Enoch is the Son of Man
Read as it stands, the ending reveals that Enoch himself is the heavenly figure of the Parables, raised up and appointed (VanderKam; Olson).
Enoch is a son of man, a righteous human

Some take "son of man" here as a plain description, "a human being" (compare Ezekiel 2:1; Casey). Charles went further and changed the text to "This is the Son of Man," pointing the title away from Enoch, though no witness known to us reads so.
The chapter is a later addition
Many scholars think chapter 71 (or 70–71) was added later by an editor who identified Enoch with the figure he had seen (Collins).

views.E: The Ethiopian church reads all of 1 Enoch as Scripture and the Son of Man of 46–69 as Christ; how it reads 71:14 is not fixed in any statement known to us.
views.H: The text says "you are." Scholars debate whether 71 is original, whether "son of man" is a title here, and how Enoch can have been hidden before creation (48:6) yet born in Genesis 5.
views.N: If the Parables are pre-Christian, 71:14 shows a Jewish writer could identify a human being with the heavenly Son of Man, as the Gospels do with Jesus.
views.J: A path toward Metatron in 3 Enoch, the exalted Enoch called "the lesser LORD."
views.W: Most Christian readers note that the New Testament never makes Enoch the Son of Man, and read the verse as Jewish speculation.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Ezekiel 1:26–28; Ezekiel 2:1; Daniel 7:9–10; Daniel 7:13; Daniel 10:9–11; Revelation 1:17; Hebrews 11:5

settings.when: after Enoch falls before the Head of Days and blesses him
settings.why: to reveal Enoch's place in heaven and to promise that all who walk his path will live with him

views: Enoch is installed as the Son of Man of the visions (VanderKam; Olson).
Enoch is called a human being born for righteousness, taking wäldä bəʾəsi in its ordinary sense (Casey).
An editor added the chapter to the Parables (Collins; Nickelsburg and VanderKam discuss it).

deep.h: How can Enoch be the Son of Man?
deep.b:
Three problems meet in 71:14. The words. The Ethiopic texts available to us (Dillmann, the EOTC Bible) read "you are" (ʾantä wəʾətu). Charles thought a Christian or Jewish scribe could not have meant to make Enoch the judge, so he emended the text to "This is the Son of Man" in the third person. Few scholars now follow him, because the change has no manuscript support. The phrase. The Parables use three Ge'ez phrases for the figure: wäldä säbʾ (46:2), wäldä bəʾəsi (69:29) and wäldä ʾəgʷalä ʾəmmäḥəyaw (62:7; 70:1). 71:14 uses wäldä bəʾəsi, literally "son of a man." Some read it as a title ("the Son of Man"); others as plain Ge'ez for "a human being." The story. The Son of Man was hidden before creation (48:3, 6), while Enoch was born in the seventh generation from Adam.

Scholars answer the third problem in different ways. VanderKam suggests that Enoch is the earthly person of whom the heavenly Son of Man is the double, so that he "becomes" what he saw. Collins thinks a later writer added 70–71 to identify Enoch with the figure. Others think the angel simply calls Enoch a righteous man, as Ezekiel is called "son of man." Ethiopian Orthodox readers take the Parables as prophecy of Christ; we have not found an official statement on this verse.

deep.title: A guess about why chapter 71 was kept
deep.b: If chapter 71 makes Enoch the Son of Man, Christian copyists had a reason to change it, yet the Ethiopic texts we have keep "you are." Copying did vary nearby (EMML 2080 at 70:1), so this is not proof. Still, it suggests the Ethiopian scribes, who read the Son of Man as Christ throughout, did not see 71:14 as a threat. They may have read "son of man" here as an ordinary human title of honor, since in ordinary Ge'ez the phrase can simply mean "a human being". If so, the debate about 71:14 is partly a modern one, created when scholars began to read the Parables apart from the church that kept them. This overlaps with the generic reading argued by Casey and with Olson's work on the Ethiopic text of 70–71; what is offered here is only the suggestion that the scribes' own reading explains why the verse survived unchanged.
